uses: Raspberry leaf has a European history going back well over a thousand years. Its best-known tradition is in late pregnancy, when the tea was drunk in the hope of an easier, quicker labor; the research behind that belief is thin and weak. As an astringent, the leaf tea was used in folk practice as a gargle for a sore mouth and throat, a wash for wounds, and a drink for loose bowels. The EMA recognizes it as a traditional remedy for period cramps, mild mouth and throat inflammation, and mild diarrhea. The fruit went into cooling summer drinks, raspberry vinegar for sore throats, wine and preserves.
energetics: Grieve described the leaf as astringent and stimulating, and the ripe fruit as cooling
caution_pregnancy: Raspberry leaf is traditionally taken in the last weeks of pregnancy to prepare for labor, but safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend it then. A few small, short studies in late pregnancy found no clear harm to mothers or babies, though some women reported diarrhea or more practice contractions (Braxton Hicks). The EMA says they are too small to show it is safe, and its small benefit doesn't outweigh possible risks to the baby. One drug-safety report describes a 2-day-old boy with seizures after his mother took it for two months to bring on labor, and in a rat study the female offspring reached puberty early. Don't take it in pregnancy on your own; use it only if your midwife or doctor advises it and oversees your care. No data exist on safety for nursing mothers or babies; avoid while breastfeeding.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions with medicines.
caution_conditions: Don't use it if you are allergic to raspberry. The EMA does not recommend it for anyone under 18. The EMA lists no known side effects, though diarrhea was reported in one study. If symptoms get worse while using it, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_duration: If period cramps or mouth and throat symptoms last more than a week, or diarrhea more than 3 days, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: The canes and leaves have prickles, so wear gloves when picking. None of our sources reports skin reactions to raspberry leaf washes.
garden_harvest_timing: The fruit ripens in summer. In October, cut out the canes that have fruited and shorten the young ones.
garden_water: Good drainage and slightly acid soil; Grieve preferred a strong loam to a light soil
notes: A suckering shrub whose canes fruit in their second year, flowering from spring into early summer. Grieve set plants about 2 feet apart in rows with plenty of air between, and started fresh beds every three or four years as old plants decline. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers, and birds take the fruit. The name idaeus recalls Mount Ida, where the ancients said the plant grew. Culpeper gives raspberry no planet and says he knew no great virtue in the leaves.
